# Results {#sec-results}

## Study population

A total of $1\,475$ women participated in the OsteoLaus study between 2010 and 2022. After applying general exclusion criteria, 317 participants were excluded: 1 had no match between OsteoLaus and CoLaus visits (as defined in Section 2.1), 49 had missing examination dates, 42 had no dairy intake data, 4 had missing covariate data for all visits, 7 reported extreme energy intakes (\< 500 or \> 3500 kcal/day), and 214 had data for fewer than 2 visits. The remaining $1\,158$ participants formed the base analytical cohort (@fig-consort).

For the handgrip strength analysis, 23 participants were excluded due to having data from fewer than 2 visits, resulting in a final sample of $1\,135$. For the ALMI analysis, 92 participants were excluded for the same reason, leaving $1\,066$. For the gait speed analysis, 358 participants were excluded because data were available at fewer than 2 visits, resulting in a final sample of 800. For the EWGSOP2 sarcopenia incidence analysis, 12 participants who were sarcopenic at T1 and 23 with data from fewer than 2 visits were excluded, leaving $1\,123$ for analysis.

Most participants in the longitudinal analyses contributed data from all 3 available study visits. In the handgrip strength analysis, 850 of $1\,135$ participants (74.9%) had data from 3 visits and 285 (25.1%) from 2. In the ALMI analysis, 812 of $1\,066$ (76.2%) had data from 3 visits and 254 (23.8%) from 2 visits. For the EWGSOP2 sarcopenia analysis, 843 of $1\,123$ (75.1%) contributed data from 3 visits and 280 (24.9%) from 2 visits. Gait speed was assessed at only 2 study visits. Therefore, all 800 participants contributed data from both visits.

![Consort flow diagram showing the number of participants enrolled, excluded at each step, and retained for analysis.](images/consort_flow-03.png){#fig-consort fig-cap="Consort flow diagram showing participants enrolled, excluded, and used in analysis." fig-alt="Flowchart showing participants recruited, reasons for exclusion, and the number retained for each outcome-specific analysis." fig-align="left"}

## Dataset matching

@fig-timepoint shows the distribution of time differences between matched CoLaus and OsteoLaus examinations across study visits. For T1 and T2, CoLaus assessments generally preceded the corresponding OsteoLaus visits, with a median difference of -316.0 days (IQR: -621.0 to -76.0) and -291.0 days (IQR: -588.5 to -5.0), respectively. In contrast, for T3, the temporal ordering was reversed, with CoLaus assessments typically occurring after OsteoLaus visits, showing a median difference of 176.5 days (IQR: -125.0 to 447.3). The fourth time point has no examination date difference since it was only an OsteoLaus visit without a matching CoLaus visit.

![Distribution of the number of days between matched CoLaus and OsteoLaus examination dates, by study visit.](images/mice_timing_violin-01.png){#fig-timepoint fig-cap="Time point alignment difference between CoLaus and OsteoLaus." fig-alt="Violin plots showing the distribution of the difference, in days, between matched CoLaus and OsteoLaus exam dates at each of the four study visits." fig-align="left"}

Follow-up assessments were conducted at approximately 2.5-year intervals. Across the shared study population, the median time from the first (T1) to the second assessment (T2) was 5.03 years (IQR: 4.96-5.14 years; range: 3.46-7.43 years). The median follow-up time from first to the third assessment (T3) was 7.57 years (IQR: 7.45-7.74 years; range: 5.95-8.79 years), while the median time from the first to the fourth assessment (T4) was 10.15 years (IQR: 9.93-10.39 years; range: 8.21-12.50 years).

For analyses of grip strength, ALMI, and EWGSOP2 sarcopenia incidence, participants contributed follow-up data over a median period of approximately 7.5 years (grip strength: 7.51 years, range 4.80-8.79; ALMI: 7.52 years, range 4.80-8.79; EWGSOP2: 7.51 years, range 4.80-8.79). For gait speed, which was assessed at T3 and T4 only, the median follow-up time was 2.58 years (IQR: 2.48-2.66 years). The interquartile ranges reflect substantial heterogeneity in follow-up timing, attributable to the varying number of study visits (two or three) per participant, as well as staggered recruitment and scheduling differences between the CoLaus and OsteoLaus cohorts.

## Imputation

Ten multiply imputed datasets were generated using chained equations. Visual inspection of diagnostic plots indicated generally good convergence of the imputation models and comparable distributions between observed and imputed values, supporting the plausibility of the imputed values. Some deviations from ideal convergence were observed for the baseline variables of left arm lean mass, right arm lean mass, left leg lean mass, and right leg lean mass. In particular, left leg lean mass showed less stable convergence across several time points, while right leg lean mass exhibited minor convergence issues at selected time points <!--# Plots to Supplements? -->. However, no substantial differences between observed and imputed value distributions were evident, suggesting that the imputations remained reasonable overall.

## Missing data

Prior to multiple imputation, 990 participants remained available for analysis after applying the shared exclusion criteria. Following MICE, the sample size increased to $1\,158$ participants. Some missing values could not be imputed because insufficient information was available from the observed data. Overall, MICE substantially reduced the proportion of missing data across most variables and study visits (@fig-missingness). At T1, missingness decreased from 6.1% to 1.2% for cumulative dairy intake, from 5.9% to 0.6% for handgrip strength, and from 16.5% to 1.8% for physical activity. Larger reductions were observed for ALMI (30.7% to 13.6%) and FNIH sarcopenia (35.2% to 13.9%). At subsequent follow-up visits, missingness was generally low and was reduced to below 1% for most variables, although ALMI and FNIH sarcopenia retained a small proportion of missing values after imputation. Total energy intake showed the largest reduction at later follow-up, decreasing from 19.5% to 0.3% at T3.

![Proportion of missing data before and after multiple imputation.](images/missing_comparison.png){#fig-missingness fig-cap="Proportion of missing data before and after multiple imputation, by variable and study visit." fig-alt="Bar charts comparing the percentage of missing values for each variable at each study visit, before versus after multiple imputation." fig-align="left"}

## Characteristics of study samples

### Baseline characteristics

Baseline characteristics according to quartiles of total dairy intake are presented in @tbl-baseline. Of the $1\,158$ women included in the base cohort before outcome-specific exclusions, $1\,119$ had available baseline dietary data and were classified into dairy intake quartiles. The remaining 39 participants had missing baseline dietary information and were therefore excluded from the quartile-based comparisons.

Baseline age and BMI distribution were similar across dairy intake quartiles. Participants in the highest quartile of dairy intake were somewhat more likely to report high physical activity (32.5% vs. 27.5% in Q1) and less likely to have hypertension (35.8% vs. 43.6% in Q1). Diabetes prevalence was low across all quartiles.

Median total dairy intake increased from 69.9 g/day (IQR 45.4 to 91.1) in Q1 to 428.8 g/day (IQR 354.4 to 537.0) in Q4, representing an approximately six-fold difference in intake. Total energy intake also increased across quartiles, from a median of 1,265 kcal/day in Q1 to 1,914 kcal/day in Q4. Low-fat dairy intake was low across all quartiles. Baseline muscle health was similar across dairy intake groups. Mean handgrip strength ranged from 23.8 to 24.5 kg, mean ALMI from 6.4 to 6.5 kg/m^2^, and gait speed was approximately 1.1 m/s across quartiles. Confirmed EWGSOP2 sarcopenia was rare, affecting fewer than 1.1% of participants in each quartile.

Included participants were generally younger and healthier than excluded participants, exhibiting lower prevalences of obesity, diabetes, and smoking, as well as higher educational attainment (@tbl-excluded-included). However, dairy intake, energy intake, physical activity, and muscle strength, muscle mass, and physical function were comparable between excluded and included participants.

### Variables over time

The distribution of categorical time-dependent covariates remained largely stable throughout follow-up (@fig-covariate-stability). <!--# TODO: insert supplementary figure -->Approximately half of participants remained in the normal BMI category at each assessment, while the prevalence of obesity increased only modestly from 14.6% at T1 to 17.5% at the final visit. Smoking patterns changed little over time, with the proportion of current smokers decreasing from 15.5% at baseline to 12.1% at the third visit. Physical activity levels were similarly stable, with approximately 30% of participants classified as highly active and around 40% as moderately active. Diabetes prevalence increased slightly from 6.0% at the first visit to 7.1% at the third visit.

Median total dairy intake declined modestly over follow-up, from 195.6 g/day (IQR 112.5 to 302.7) at T1 to 193.6 g/day (IQR 114.6 to 303.8) at the second visit and 182.4 g/day (IQR 105.7 to 270.4) at the third visit (@fig-dairy-trend). Similar patterns were observed for all dairy subtypes, indicating only modest changes in consumption over time. Median total energy intake also decreased slightly, from 1,561 kcal/day (IQR 1,208 to 1,981) at T1 to 1,536 kcal/day (IQR 1,202 to 1,933) at T2 and 1,455 kcal/day (IQR 1,181 to 1,792) at T3. The alluvial plot demonstrated that most participants remained within the same dairy intake quartile throughout follow-up (@fig-alluvial).

![Median total dairy intake and dairy subtype intake over follow-up, T1-T3](images/boxplot_dairy_total_gday_cumavg.png){#fig-dairy-trend fig-align="left"}

![Alluvial plot of dairy intake quartile membership across study visits, showing the stability of quartile assignment over follow-up.](images/alluvial_dairy_quartile_baseline.png){#fig-alluvial fig-align="left"}

No clear age-related trend in dairy intake was observed (@fig-dairy-age). Mean dairy consumption remained relatively stable across the age range, despite some fluctuations at the oldest ages that likely reflected smaller sample sizes. The wide error bars across all ages further indicate substantial between-participant variability in dairy consumption. Age-related declines were observed for handgrip strength, gait speed, and ALMI. However, the decline in ALMI appeared attenuated and more variable at older ages, likely reflecting smaller sample sizes and increased heterogeneity in this age group.

![Mean total dairy intake by age, with error bars showing variability between participants.](images/trajectory_dairy_total_gday_cumavg.png){#fig-dairy-age fig-align="left"}

### Outcome trajectories

Grip strength showed a clear age-related decline from 50 to 90 years old (@fig-trajectory-hgs). Mean grip strength was approximately 26 kg between ages 50 and 60, decreased gradually to around 24 kg by age 70, and declined more steeply thereafter, reaching approximately 21 kg at age 76 to 79 and below 20 kg after age 80. Overall, mean grip strength decreased from 26.8 kg at age 50 to 18.5 kg at age 80, corresponding to an absolute decline of approximately 8.3 kg (31%). While some year-to-year fluctuations were observed, likely due to varying sample sizes, the overall trajectory was consistently downward with advancing age.

![Mean handgrip strength by age, ages 50-90 years.](images/trajectory_HGS_MAX.png){#fig-trajectory-hgs fig-align="left"}

Gait speed remained relatively stable throughout early older adulthood, with mean values around 1.15 m/s to 1.25 m/s between ages 57 and 70 (@fig-trajectory-gait). A gradual decline became apparent from approximately age 70 onward, with mean gait speed falling below 1.10 m/s by age 71 to 75 and reaching approximately 1.00 m/s around age 80. At the oldest ages, gait speed declined more markedly, reaching values below 0.90 m/s in participants aged 83 years and older. Overall, the trajectory suggests preservation of walking performance until the early seventies, followed by progressive functional decline with increasing age.

![Mean gait speed by age.](images/trajectory_gait_speed.png){#fig-trajectory-gait}

ALMI exhibited a more gradual age-related decline than the functional measures (@fig-trajectory-almi). Mean ALMI was approximately 6.6 kg/m² to 6.8 kg/m² in participants younger than 55 years and decreased steadily with increasing age. By age 70, mean ALMI had fallen to approximately 6.2 kg/m², representing a decline of about 0.5 kg/m² (8%) from age 50. Thereafter, ALMI remained relatively stable around 6.0 kg/m² to 6.2 kg/m², with greater variability at older ages due to smaller sample sizes. Compared with grip strength and gait speed, the decline in muscle mass appeared less pronounced, suggesting that age-related losses in muscle function exceeded losses in muscle quantity.

![Mean ALMI by age.](images/trajectory_ALM_HT2_harmonised.png){#fig-trajectory-almi}

The prevalence of confirmed EWGSOP2 sarcopenia increased from 0.8% at T1 to 3.0% at the third visit and 3.4% (confirmed or severe sarcopenia combined) at the final visit. Similarly, FNIH-defined sarcopenia increased from 0.5% at T1 to 2.5% at later visits.

### Relationship between dairy intake and muscle health outcomes

Scatter plots indicated only weak descriptive differences in muscle outcomes across cumulative dairy intake quartiles (@fig-scatter-outcomes). For handgrip strength, mean values at T1 increased slightly from Q1 to Q3, while the highest quartile (Q4) showed greater variability, likely reflecting fewer observations at higher cumulative dairy intake levels. At T2 and T3, mean handgrip strength increased modestly from Q1 to Q2 and remained largely unchanged across the higher quartiles. Across all time points, substantial inter-individual variability in handgrip strength was observed within each dairy intake quartile, indicating considerable overlap between exposure groups.

For ALMI, a small increase in mean values was observed from Q1 to Q2 at T1, with little further change across the remaining quartiles. Similar to handgrip strength, ALMI showed a broad distribution within each dairy intake quartile at all time points, suggesting high between-participant variability.

Gait speed demonstrated a comparable pattern at both available assessments, with a modest increase in mean gait speed from Q1 to Q2 followed by little variation across Q2 to Q4. Individual gait speed values also showed substantial overlap between dairy intake quartiles.

## Association between dairy intake and handgrip strength

### Primary exposure cumulative average total dairy intake and handgrip strength

In the adjusted linear mixed-effects model for handgrip strength, cumulative average total dairy intake was positively associated with handgrip strength over follow-up (@tbl-HGS-main). Each 100 g/day higher intake was associated with a 0.207 kg higher handgrip strength ($\beta$ = 0.207, 95% CI 0.053 to 0.360, p = 0.009). Handgrip strength decreased over time ($\beta$ = -0.140 kg per year, 95% CI -0.184 to -0.095, p \< 0.001) and was significantly lower with higher baseline age ($\beta$ = -2.949, 95% CI -3.328 to -2.570, p \< 0.001). Compared with participants with normal BMI, those who were overweight had higher handgrip strength ($\beta$ = 0.646, 95% CI 0.150 to 1.141, p = 0.011), whereas underweight participants had lower handgrip strength ($\beta$ = -1.679, 95% CI -3.195 to -0.163, p = 0.030). Participants with high educational attainment also had higher handgrip strength than those with low education ($\beta$ = 1.753, 95% CI 0.780 to 2.726, p \< 0.001). No significant associations were observed for obesity, smoking status, physical activity, diabetes, or total energy intake (@tbl-HGS-main).

### Sensitivity analysis for handgrip strength

Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that the results were robust for the linear mixed-effect model with handgrip strength. Excluding participants with extreme dairy intake (\>1000 g/day; n = 5) did not materially alter the association between cumulative average dairy intake and handgrip strength ($\beta$ = 0.177, 95% CI 0.014 to 0.341, p = 0.034). Similarly, excluding the top 1% most influential observations identified using Cook's distance (n = 31) produced comparable estimates, with a larger effect estimate ($\beta$ = 0.239, 95% CI 0.086 to 0.392, p = 0.002), indicating that the observed association was not driven by extreme or influential observations and was robust to the exclusion of high-leverage data points.

### Model fit and variance decomposition for handgrip strength

The linear mixed-effects model indicated substantial differences in handgrip strength between participants. The random intercept variance was 14.76 (SD = 3.84), demonstrating considerable variation in baseline handgrip strength across individuals, while the residual variance was 14.35 (SD = 3.79). The fixed effects explained 16.3% of the variation in handgrip strength (marginal R^2^ = 0.163). Including the participant-specific random intercept increased the explained variance to 58.7% (conditional R^2^ = 0.587), indicating that a large proportion of the variability in handgrip strength reflected stable differences between individuals rather than the measured covariates alone.

### Secondary exposures for handgrip strength

Among dairy subtypes, statistically significant positive associations with handgrip strength were observed for fermented dairy ($\beta$ = 0.219 kg per 100 g/day, 95% CI 0.028 to 0.409, p = 0.024) and high-fat dairy ($\beta$ = 0.221 kg per 100 g/day, 95% CI 0.043 to 0.399, p = 0.015). No statistically significant associations were found for non-fermented dairy or low-fat dairy intake (@tbl-HGS-sec).

When analysed by dairy intake quartiles, participants in the third quartile had higher handgrip strength than those in the lowest quartile (Q3 vs Q1: $\beta$ = 0.981 kg, 95% CI 0.350 to 1.612, p = 0.002). No significant differences were observed for Q2 or Q4 compared with Q1 (@tbl-HGS-sec). However, after excluding the 31 most influential observations identified by Cook's distance (top 1%), participants in both Q2 ($\beta$ = 0.608 kg, 95% CI 0.052 to 1.164, p = 0.032) and Q4 ($\beta$ = 0.710 kg, 95% CI 0.012 to 1.408, p = 0.046) also exhibited significantly higher handgrip strength than those in Q1, while the association for Q3 remained significant ($\beta$ = 1.128 kg, 95% CI 0.512 to 1.744, p \< 0.001). These findings suggest that the positive association between dairy intake and handgrip strength was strengthened after removal of influential observations. Adherence to dairy consumption guidelines ($\ge$ 2 servings/day) was not associated with handgrip strength (@tbl-HGS-sec).

## Association between dairy intake and ALMI

### Primary exposure cumulative average total dairy intake and ALMI

The fully adjusted linear mixed-effects model showed that a 100 g/day higher dairy intake was associated with a non-significant increase in ALMI of 0.010 kg/m² ($\beta$ = 0.010, 95% CI -0.006 to 0.027, p = 0.210; @tbl-ALMI-main). Associations with covariates were statistically significant but small in magnitude. ALMI declined over time ($\beta$ = -0.046 kg/m² per year, 95% CI -0.050 to -0.042, p \< 0.001) and was lower among participants of higher baseline age ($\beta$ = -0.126, 95% CI -0.176 to -0.077, p \< 0.001). Former smokers had slightly higher ALMI than never smokers ($\beta$ = 0.083, 95% CI 0.010 to 0.156, p = 0.027), whereas no association was observed for current smoking. Participants with high physical activity had slightly higher ALMI than those with low physical activity ($\beta$ = 0.097, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.192, p = 0.045), while medium physical activity was not associated with ALMI. A significant association of larger magnitude was observed for BMI category. Compared with participants of normal weight, underweight participants had lower ALMI ($\beta$ = -0.320, 95% CI -0.451 to -0.189, p \< 0.001), whereas overweight ($\beta$ = 0.407, 95% CI 0.361 to 0.453, p \< 0.001) and obese participants ($\beta$ = 0.906, 95% CI 0.835 to 0.976, p \< 0.001) had higher ALMI.

### Sensitivity analysis for ALMI

Results were unchanged after excluding participants with extreme dairy intake (\>1000 g/day; n = 5) and influential observations identified by Cook's distance (n = 23). Sensitivity analyses for ALMI therefore indicated that the findings were robust.

### Model fit and variance decomposition for ALMI

The model shows that most of the variation in the outcome comes from differences between individuals, while the remaining variation is within individuals over time. Specifically, the variability between participants (random intercept) is relatively large (variance = 0.31), meaning people differ quite a lot in their baseline levels. The within-person variability (residual variance = 0.07) is smaller, meaning that repeated measurements within the same person are more consistent.

Overall model fit is good. The fixed effects explain about 27% of the variation (marginal R^2^ = 0.27), while the full model including individual differences explains about 87% (conditional R^2^ = 0.87). This indicates that individual-level differences account for most of the variability in the data.

### Secondary exposures for ALMI

No statistically significant associations were observed between dairy intake and ALMI, regardless of exposure specification (@tbl-ALMI-sec). Continuous analyses showed effect estimates close to zero for fermented, non-fermented, high-fat, and low-fat dairy intake. There was a gradual increase in effect estimates across dairy intake quartiles compared with Q1 (Q2: $\beta$ = 0.012; Q3: $\beta$ = 0.034; Q4: $\beta$ = 0.062), suggesting a weak upward trend. However, all confidence intervals included zero and none of the comparisons reached statistical significance.

Dairy guideline adherence ($\ge$ 2 servings/day) was also not associated with ALMI (@tbl-ALMI-sec). Overall, findings were consistent across exposure definitions and did not support an association between dairy intake and ALMI.

|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Continuous exposures** |  |  |  |  |
| Fermented dairy | Per 100 g/day | 0.008 | -0.012, 0.028 | 0.437 |
| Non-fermented dairy | Per 100 g/day | 0.019 | -0.011, 0.050 | 0.218 |
| High-fat dairy | Per 100 g/day | 0.007 | -0.012, 0.026 | 0.489 |

### Secondary outcome for ALMI

In the sensitivity analysis using an alternative ALM index (standardized by BMI instead of height squared), higher cumulative dairy intake was positively associated with ALM index. The association was small in magnitude but statistically significant ($\beta$ = 0.003, 95% CI 0.001 to 0.005, p = 0.005).

## Association between dairy intake and gait speed

### Primary exposure cumulative average total dairy intake for gait speed

For gait speed, lagged cumulative average total dairy intake showed no association in the fully adjusted linear mixed model (@tbl-gait-main). A 100 g/day higher intake corresponded to a negligible difference of 0.001 m/s in gait speed (95% CI -0.005 to 0.007, p = 0.748).

Gait speed declined with higher baseline age ($\beta$ = -0.122 m/s, 95% CI -0.138 to -0.105, p \< 0.001). Compared with normal weight, overweight and obesity were associated with slower gait speed ($\beta$ = -0.062 and -0.119 m/s, respectively; both p \< 0.001), while underweight showed no difference. Higher educational attainment was associated with faster gait speed (high vs low: $\beta$ = 0.058 m/s, 95% CI 0.017 to 0.099, p = 0.006). Diabetes was associated with lower gait speed ($\beta$ = -0.076 m/s, 95% CI -0.119 to -0.034, p \< 0.001). Time since baseline, smoking status, and physical activity were not significantly associated with gait speed.

### Sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analyses for gait speed showed that results were robust. Excluding participants with extreme dairy intake (\>1000 g/day; n = 2) did not materially change the association between cumulative average dairy intake and ALMI ($\beta$ = 0.003, 95% CI -0.004 to 0.010, p = 0.349). Similarly, exclusion of influential observations identified by Cook's distance (n = 14) yielded comparable estimates ($\beta$ = 0.001, 95% CI -0.005 to 0.007, p = 0.731).

### Model fit and variance decomposition for gait speed

The linear mixed-effects model showed moderate explanatory power of the fixed effects, with a marginal R^2^ of 0.247. Including random effects substantially improved model fit, yielding a conditional R^2^ of 0.655, indicating that accounting for between-individual differences explains a large share of the outcome variability.

The variance of the random intercept was 0.0167 (SD = 0.129), while the residual variance was 0.0142 (SD = 0.119). These values are of similar magnitude, suggesting that variability between individuals is comparable to variability within individuals over time, with a slightly larger contribution from between-subject differences after adjustment for covariates.

### Secondary exposures for gait speed

No statistically significant associations were observed for any dairy subtype (@tbl-gait-sec). Across all exposure definitions, effect estimates were small and consistently centered around the null, indicating no meaningful relationship between dairy intake and gait speed in this model.

## Model diagnostics

Model assumptions were evaluated using standard diagnostic plots for all three outcomes (@fig-diagnostics-hgs, @fig-diagnostics-almi, and @fig-diagnostics-gait). Q–Q plots indicated approximately normally distributed residuals for handgrip strength, ALMI, and gait speed, with only minor deviations at the distribution tails. These deviations were reduced after excluding influential observations, resulting in improved tail behavior. Scale-location plots suggested generally constant variance of residuals across fitted values. However, a mild U-shaped pattern was observed for handgrip strength and gait speed, consistent with slight heteroskedasticity. For ALMI, heteroskedasticity was mainly present at higher fitted values and was attenuated after exclusion of influential observations.

![HGS LMM Diagnostics](images/HGS_MAX___dairy_100g__linear______main_main_diagnostics.png){#fig-diagnostics-hgs}

![ALMI LMM Diagnosics](images/ALM_HT2_harmonised___dairy_100g__linear______main_main_diagnostics.png){#fig-diagnostics-almi}

![Gait speed diagnostics](images/gait_speed___dairy_100g_lag__linear______main_main_diagnostics.png){#fig-diagnostics-gait}

Residuals versus fitted values plots indicated systematic patterns across all outcomes, characterized by a tendency for residuals to increase with higher fitted values and decrease at lower fitted values. This suggests some degree of model misspecification, most pronounced for handgrip strength, less pronounced for ALMI, and present to a lesser extent for gait speed. Standard transformations (log, square-root), inclusion of polynomial terms, natural splines for dairy intake, dairy–time interaction terms, adjustment for height and weight, within- and between-person decomposition of dairy intake, alternative random-effects structures, variance function modeling, generalized additive mixed models with smooth dairy terms, polynomial terms for age, and exclusion of influential observations did not materially improve this pattern.

To assess the impact of these deviations on inference, cluster-robust (sandwich) standard errors were applied. The estimated associations between cumulative average dairy intake and all three outcomes remained unchanged in magnitude and inference for handgrip strength ($\beta$ = 0.207, p = 0.011), ALMI ($\beta$ = 0.010, p = 0.224), and gait speed ($\beta$ = 0.001, p = 0.778), indicating robustness of the main findings to heteroskedasticity and mild model misspecification. Overall, while point estimates and inference were stable under robust variance estimation, diagnostic plots indicate that model fit is not perfect. Therefore, results should be interpreted as population-average associations that are robust to variance heterogeneity rather than exact model-based functional relationships.

## Association between dairy intake and incident sarcopenia

During a mean follow-up of 7814 person-years, 50 incident cases of sarcopenia were observed for the EWGSOP2 definition. This corresponds to an overall incidence rate of approximately 0.64 cases per 100 person-years. The number of incident sarcopenia cases was similar across the first three dairy intake quartiles but was higher in the highest quartile (Q4). Correspondingly, crude incidence rates ranged from 5.14 to 6.34 per 1000 person-years in Q1 to Q3 and increased to 8.85 per 1000 person-years in Q4 (@tbl-incidence-rate).

Model discrimination was moderate to good. The C-index was 0.79 (95% CI 0.735-0.845) for the categorical dairy intake model. Likelihood ratio tests indicated that the full models provided a statistically significant improvement over null models.

Sensitivity analyses using cumulative average dairy intake as a continuous exposure produced results consistent with the primary categorical model. In the fully adjusted Cox model, the association per 100 g/day increase was close to null (HR = 1.0004, 95% CI: 0.9988, 1.0019, p = 0.633), with no statistically significant effect. Modelling dairy intake using natural cubic splines (3 degrees of freedom) did not improve model fit compared with the linear specification (likelihood ratio test: \$\\chi\$^2^(2) = 2.49, p = 0.288), indicating no evidence for a non-linear dose–response relationship (@tbl-spline-cox). A dose-response plot is available in the supplementary material (@fig-dose-response). Overall, dairy intake was not associated with incident sarcopenia across functional forms of exposure modelling.

## Model assumptions and diagnostics

The conditions specified by Vittinghoff & McCulloch (2007) [@vittinghoff2007] for relaxing the EPV rule were judged to be met: quartile groups were approximately balanced (n = 273–290 participants per quartile), and the observed hazard ratios were modest for the main model (HR range 0.797–1.163 across quartiles), without evidence of extreme effect sizes or rare exposure categories. The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using Schoenfeld residuals and was not violated in any model (global test p \> 0.05 in all cases). Multicollinearity was low, with all variance inflation factors below 5. Model calibration assessed using Cox-Snell residuals indicated acceptable overall fit, although minor deviations from the 45-degree line were observed at higher cumulative hazard levels. No major violations were observed in martingale residuals or functional form diagnostics. However, visual inspection suggested slight lack of fit at higher exposure ranges, particularly for categorical models. Most censoring was administrative, occurring because participants remained free of sarcopenia at the end of follow-up, and is therefore likely to be non-informative. However, 15.2% of participants were lost to follow-up before the third visit. For these individuals, censoring may have been informative if their probability of dropout was related to their underlying risk of developing sarcopenia.
